sentences.nl: In deze les oefenen we de grammatica, van #dutchgrammar les 11 en 12, over getallen en het meervoud.
sentences.en: In this lesson, we practice the grammar from #dutchgrammar lessons 11 and 12 about numbers and the plural.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• In this lesson practice we the grammar, of #dutchgrammar lesson 11 and 12, about numbers and the plural.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "In deze les" (In this lesson) sets the context and is a prepositional phrase indicating time or setting.  
• "oefenen we" (we practice) is a simple present tense verb structure. In Dutch, the verb often comes second in main clauses.  
• "de grammatica, van #dutchgrammar les 11 en 12," (the grammar, of #dutchgrammar lesson 11 and 12,) includes a possessive structure using "van" to indicate "of."  
• "over getallen en het meervoud" (about numbers and the plural) uses "over" to indicate the topic of study.

Examples:  
– "In deze cursus leren we veel over cultuur." (In this course, we learn a lot about culture.)  
– "Oefenen jullie de uitspraak elke dag?" (Do you practice pronunciation every day?)  
– "Het boek van mijn broer is interessant." (The book of my brother is interesting.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "In die workshop bespreken we de verschillende dialecten van Nederland." (In that workshop, we discuss the different dialects of the Netherlands.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• The use of hashtags like "#dutchgrammar" indicates the integration of social media and online resources in language learning, reflecting modern educational practices.

sentences.nl: Martin en Marieke zijn op de markt.
sentences.en: Martin and Marieke are at the market.

sentences.nl: Ze gaan eten kopen.
sentences.en: They are going to buy food.

sentences.nl: Daarna gaat Martin voor Marieke koken.
sentences.en: Afterwards, Martin is going to cook for Marieke.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Afterwards goes Martin for Marieke to cook.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Daarna" is an adverb meaning "afterwards" and often used to indicate a sequence of events.  
• "Gaat" is the present tense of "gaan" (to go), which is used here as an auxiliary verb to indicate a future action.  
• "Voor" is a preposition meaning "for," indicating the beneficiary of the action.  
• Word order: In Dutch, the main verb ("koken") is placed at the end of the sentence after the auxiliary verb ("gaat").  

Examples:  
• Daarna gaat zij naar haar werk. (Afterwards she goes to her work.)  
• Daarna wil ik een boek lezen. (Afterwards I want to read a book.)  
• Hij gaat voor zijn moeder boodschappen doen. (He is going to do groceries for his mother.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Daarna gaat Jan voor zijn vrienden een taart bakken. (Afterwards Jan is going to bake a cake for his friends.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Cooking for someone in the Netherlands can be a gesture of care and hospitality, often reflecting a personal relationship or special occasion.

sentences.nl: Wat wil je eten? vraagt Martin aan Marieke.
sentences.en: What do you want to eat? Martin asks Marieke.

sentences.en: Uh...

sentences.nl: Wat vind je lekker? — Ik hou van Hollandse kost.
sentences.en: What do you like? — I love Dutch food.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• What find you tasty? — I love Dutch food.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Wat vind je lekker?" follows the Dutch question structure where the verb ("vind") comes before the subject ("je").  
• "Ik hou van" means "I love" or "I like" and is commonly used to express preferences. "Van" is a preposition here that connects the verb "hou" with the object of affection.  
• "Hollandse kost" refers to traditional Dutch cuisine. "Kost" is an older term for food.  

Extra phrases:  
• "Wat vind je leuk?" (What do you find fun?)  
• "Ik hou van muziek." (I love music.)  
• "Hij houdt van zijn werk." (He loves his work.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Wat eet je graag?" (What do you like to eat?)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Hollandse kost typically includes dishes like stamppot, erwtensoep (pea soup), and hutspot. These are often hearty, simple meals that reflect the agricultural history of the Netherlands.

sentences.nl: Een stukje vlees, aardappelen en groente.
sentences.en: A piece of meat, potatoes, and vegetables.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• A piece of meat, potatoes, and vegetables.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• This sentence is a simple noun phrase listing three food items. "Een stukje vlees" uses the diminutive form "stukje," which implies a small piece or portion.  
• The nouns "aardappelen" (potatoes) and "groente" (vegetables) are plural, but in Dutch, "groente" can be both singular and plural depending on context.  
• Examples:  
  - Een stukje kaas, brood en wijn. (A piece of cheese, bread, and wine.)  
  - Een glaasje water, koffie en thee. (A small glass of water, coffee, and tea.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Een stukje taart, koffie en slagroom. (A piece of cake, coffee, and whipped cream.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• The combination of "een stukje vlees, aardappelen en groente" is a traditional Dutch meal format, often referred to as "AVG" for "Aardappelen, Vlees, Groente" (Potatoes, Meat, Vegetables). This was a common dinner structure in Dutch households, especially in the mid-20th century.

sentences.nl: Dan gaan we eerst naar de groenteboer.
sentences.en: Then we will first go to the greengrocer.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Then go we first to the greengrocer.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Dan" is an adverb meaning "then," often used to indicate the next step in a sequence.  
• "Gaan" is the verb "to go" in the present tense, positioned second in the sentence due to Dutch word order rules (subject-verb inversion for questions and certain statements).  
• "Eerst" means "first," used to indicate the first action or step.  
• "Naar" is a preposition meaning "to," used for direction or movement towards a place.  
• "Groenteboer" is a compound noun combining "groente" (vegetables) and "boer" (farmer), meaning "greengrocer."

Extra examples:  
• "Dan eten we samen." (Then we eat together.)  
• "Eerst maak ik het huis schoon." (First, I clean the house.)  
• "We gaan naar de bakker." (We go to the baker.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Dan drinken we koffie bij de bakker." (Then we drink coffee at the bakery.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, visiting the "groenteboer" is a common activity, as many people prefer to buy fresh produce from local vendors rather than supermarkets.

sentences.nl: Verse grote tomaten…, uien in de aanbieding…, mooie groene bonen…
sentences.en: Fresh large tomatoes..., onions on sale..., nice green beans...
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Fresh large tomatoes..., onions on sale..., beautiful green beans...

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The sentence consists of noun phrases that describe items in a market or store setting. The ellipses suggest a list or continuation.  
• "Verse" is an adjective meaning "fresh" and agrees in form with "grote tomaten" (large tomatoes).  
• "In de aanbieding" is a common phrase meaning "on sale." It uses the preposition "in" to indicate a state or condition.  
• Example: "Appels in de aanbieding" (Apples on sale).  
• "Mooie groene bonen" uses adjectives "mooie" (beautiful) and "groene" (green) before the noun "bonen" (beans).  
• Example: "Mooie rode rozen" (Beautiful red roses).  
• Example: "Grote gele bananen" (Large yellow bananas).

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Verse aardbeien, sappige perziken, heerlijke druiven..." (Fresh strawberries, juicy peaches, delicious grapes...)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch markets, it's common to see signs listing fresh produce and specials using descriptive phrases like these. Shoppers often look for "aanbiedingen" (sales) to find good deals.

sentences.nl: Hoeveel aardappelen zullen we kopen? — We zijn met twee personen.
sentences.en: How many potatoes shall we buy? — There are two of us.

sentences.nl: 10 aardappelen alstublieft, één, twee, drie, vier, vijf, zes, zeven, acht, negen, tien
sentences.en: 10 potatoes please, one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• 10 potatoes please, one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The word "alstublieft" is a formal way of saying "please" in Dutch and is often used when speaking to strangers or in formal settings. The informal version is "alsjeblieft."  
• In Dutch, numbers are used exactly like in English when counting or listing items.  
• Example phrases:  
  - "Drie appels alstublieft." (Three apples please.)  
  - "Vijf boeken alsjeblieft." (Five books please.)  
  - "Twee kopjes koffie alstublieft." (Two cups of coffee please.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Twaalf bloemen alsjeblieft, één, twee, drie, vier, vijf, zes, zeven, acht, negen, tien, elf, twaalf." (Twelve flowers please, one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, eleven, twelve.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, it is common to use "alstublieft" or "alsjeblieft" in transactions to be polite, whether you are asking for something or handing something over.

sentences.nl: Alstublieft!
sentences.en: Please!

sentences.nl: Hoeveel kost dat? — 920 gram
sentences.en: How much does that cost? — 920 grams
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• How much cost that? — 920 gram

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Hoeveel kost dat?" is a simple question structure in Dutch. "Hoeveel" means "how much," "kost" is the third-person singular form of "kosten" (to cost), and "dat" means "that."  
• The word order is typical for a Dutch question: question word + verb + subject.  
• "920 gram" is a straightforward way to express weight in Dutch, using the metric system.

Examples:  
- "Hoeveel kost dit boek?" (How much does this book cost?)  
- "Hoeveel kost een ticket naar Amsterdam?" (How much does a ticket to Amsterdam cost?)  
- "Hoeveel gram suiker heb je nodig?" (How many grams of sugar do you need?)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Hoeveel kost deze fiets?" (How much does this bike cost?)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, the metric system is used for weights and measures, so grams and kilograms are standard for measuring food and other items.

sentences.nl: Dat is 2 euro 50.
sentences.en: That is 2 euros 50.

sentences.nl: Anders nog iets meneer? — Marieke, welke groente wil je? — Ik vind courgettes lekker.
sentences.en: Anything else, sir? — Marieke, which vegetable would you like? — I like zucchinis.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Anything else mister? — Marieke, which vegetable want you? — I find zucchinis tasty.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Anders nog iets:** This phrase is a common way to ask if someone needs anything else, often used in service contexts.  
• **Welke groente wil je?:** "Welke" is used to ask "which" or "what" when referring to a specific item from a group. Note the verb-second word order: subject "je" follows the verb "wil."  
• **Ik vind courgettes lekker:** The verb "vinden" (to find) is used to express opinions about tastes, followed by an adjective like "lekker" (tasty).

Examples:  
- **Anders nog iets, mevrouw?** (Anything else, ma'am?)  
- **Welke kleur vind jij mooi?** (Which color do you find beautiful?)  
- **Ik vind honden leuk.** (I find dogs nice.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• **Anders nog iets, meneer de Vries?** (Anything else, Mr. de Vries?)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• The phrase "Anders nog iets?" is very common in Dutch shops, markets, and restaurants. It reflects a polite and customer-focused service style.

sentences.nl: Mag ik 2 courgettes? — 2 courgettes voor meneertje
sentences.en: May I have 2 zucchinis? — 2 zucchinis for the little gentleman.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Mag ik 2 courgettes? — 2 courgettes voor meneertje  
(Can I have 2 zucchinis? — 2 zucchinis for the little man)

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Mag ik" introduces a polite request, similar to "May I" or "Can I."  
• "Courgettes" is the Dutch word for zucchinis, used in the plural form here.  
• "Meneertje" is a diminutive form of "meneer" (gentleman), often used affectionately or humorously.  
• Word order: The sentence begins with a verb ("Mag") because it's a question.  
• Examples:  
  - "Mag ik een kop koffie?" (Can I have a cup of coffee?)  
  - "Heb je de courgettes gezien?" (Have you seen the zucchinis?)  
  - "Voor meneertje is alles klaar." (Everything is ready for the little man.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Mag ik een appel? — Een appel voor de dame." (Can I have an apple? — An apple for the lady.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, using diminutives like "meneertje" can be a friendly or playful way to refer to someone, often in informal situations.

sentences.nl: Even kijken…
sentences.en: Let's see…
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Even kijken…  
  (Just look...)

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Even" is an informal word used to indicate a short pause, similar to "just" or "quickly" in English.  
• "Kijken" is the verb "to look" or "to see." In this context, it implies taking a moment to check or consider something.  
• The phrase "Even kijken" is often used when someone is about to check or look into something briefly.

• Extra phrases:  
  - "Even wachten alstublieft." (Please wait a moment.)  
  - "Ik ga even zitten." (I am going to sit down for a moment.)  
  - "Even bellen." (Just calling quickly.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Even nadenken…" (Just thinking for a moment…)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• The phrase "Even kijken" is often used in everyday situations in the Netherlands, such as when browsing or deciding on something in a shop, or when someone needs a moment to process information. It reflects a casual and relaxed approach to decision-making.

sentences.nl: 2 euro 50, plus 3 euro 25, is 5 euro 75
sentences.en: 2 euros 50, plus 3 euros 25, is 5 euros 75
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• 2 euro 50, plus 3 euro 25, is 5 euro 75

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The sentence uses numbers with currency units, which are expressed in a straightforward manner: number + "euro" + cents.  
• "Plus" is used just like in English to indicate addition.  
• The sentence structure is simple and mirrors the arithmetic operation directly.

• Examples:  
  - "10 euro 99, plus 4 euro 01, is 15 euro." (10 euros 99, plus 4 euros 01, is 15 euros.)  
  - "7 euro 30, plus 2 euro 70, is 10 euro." (7 euros 30, plus 2 euros 70, is 10 euros.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "5 euro 10, plus 6 euro 40, is 11 euro 50." (5 euros 10, plus 6 euros 40, is 11 euros 50.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, the euro is the standard currency, and prices are often rounded to the nearest cent. It's common to see prices written in this format, especially when dealing with cash transactions or receipts.

sentences.nl: Alstublieft, hier is een briefje van 10.
sentences.en: Here you go, here is a 10 note.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Please, here is a note of 10.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Alstublieft" is a formal way to say "please" or "here you go," commonly used when handing something over.  
• "Hier is" means "here is," which is a straightforward way to present or show something.  
• "Een briefje van 10" refers to a "note of 10," meaning a 10 euro bill. In Dutch, currency notes are often referred to with "briefje van" followed by the amount.

• Example 1: "Alstublieft, hier is uw koffie." (Please, here is your coffee.)  
• Example 2: "Hier is mijn adres." (Here is my address.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Alstublieft, hier is de sleutel van de kamer." (Please, here is the key to the room.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, using "alstublieft" when handing over money or items is considered polite, especially in formal settings like in shops or restaurants.

sentences.nl: Dan krijgt u van mij wisselgeld.
sentences.en: Then you will receive change from me.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Then gets you from me change money.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Dan" typically means "then" or "at that time," often used to indicate a sequence.  
• "Krijgt" is the third person singular form of "krijgen" (to get/receive), in the present tense.  
• "U" is the formal form of "you," used in polite or formal situations.  
• "Van mij" means "from me," indicating the source or giver.  
• "Wisselgeld" means "change" in the sense of money returned after a transaction.

Extra phrases:  
• "Dan ga ik naar huis." (Then I go home.)  
• "U krijgt een cadeau van mij." (You receive a gift from me.)  
• "Waar is mijn wisselgeld?" (Where is my change?)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Dan geef ik u de sleutel." (Then I give you the key.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, using "u" is a sign of respect and is typically used when talking to strangers, elders, or in formal situations.

sentences.nl: 10 euro min 5 euro 75, is 4 euro 25
sentences.en: 10 euros minus 5 euros 75 is 4 euros 25
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• 10 euro minus 5 euro 75, is 4 euro 25

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• This sentence demonstrates a basic arithmetic expression using "minus" and "is" to indicate subtraction and the result.  
• "Euro" is used both in singular and plural without changes in Dutch, similar to English when referring to amounts.  
• The Dutch word "is" is used here just like in English to equate the result.

Extra phrases:  
• "20 euro min 10 euro is 10 euro." (20 euros minus 10 euros is 10 euros.)  
• "15 min 7 is 8." (15 minus 7 is 8.)  
• "Het huis kost 300.000 euro." (The house costs 300,000 euros.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "8 euro min 3 euro 50, is 4 euro 50." (8 euros minus 3 euros 50, is 4 euros 50.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Euro is the currency used in the Netherlands, and prices are often mentioned to the cent, much like in the sentence provided.

sentences.nl: Alstublieft: 2 munten van 2 euro, en 2 muntjes:, één van 20 cent, en één van 5 cent.
sentences.en: Here you go: 2 coins of 2 euros, and 2 small coins: one of 20 cents, and one of 5 cents.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Please: 2 coins of 2 euro, and 2 small coins: one of 20 cents, and one of 5 cents.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Alstublieft" is a polite form of "please" or "here you go" used when offering something.  
• "Munten" is the plural form of "munt," meaning "coins." The use of "van" indicates possession or composition ("of").  
• "Muntjes" is a diminutive form of "munt," often implying smaller coins or a more informal context. The suffix "-jes" is commonly used to form diminutives.  
• Example phrases:  
  - "Alstublieft, uw koffie." (Here you go, your coffee.)  
  - "Ik heb drie munten van één euro." (I have three coins of one euro.)  
  - "Hij gaf me een muntje voor de automaat." (He gave me a small coin for the vending machine.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Alstublieft: een brief van tien euro en twee muntjes van vijftig cent." (Here you go: a ten euro note and two small coins of fifty cents.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, it's common to use cash, particularly coins, for small transactions, though digital payments are increasingly popular. "Alstublieft" is a polite term used in various contexts, from formal settings to everyday transactions.

sentences.nl: Wat vind jij lekker Martin? — Biefstuk!
sentences.en: What do you like, Martin? — Steak!
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• What find you tasty Martin? — Steak!

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Wat vind jij lekker" is a common way to ask someone what they like or find tasty. "Vind" is the present tense of "vinden" (to find), and "lekker" means tasty or nice.  
• The subject "jij" (you) follows the verb "vind" due to the question structure.  
• "Biefstuk" means steak, a common dish in the Netherlands.  

Additional Examples:  
• "Wat vind jij leuk om te doen?" (What do you like to do?)  
• "Vind je deze film goed?" (Do you find this movie good?)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Wat vind jij van dit boek?" (What do you think of this book?)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, steak (biefstuk) is often served as a simple dish with potatoes and vegetables. The Dutch have a straightforward approach to meals, focusing on quality ingredients.

sentences.nl: Lust jij dat? — Ja natuurlijk!
sentences.en: Do you like that? — Yes, of course!
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Lust jij dat? — Ja natuurlijk!  
  (Do you desire that? — Yes, of course!)

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Lust" is a modal verb meaning "to desire" or "to like," often used with food or drinks.  
• "Jij" is the informal "you," often emphasizing the subject.  
• "Ja natuurlijk" is a common phrase meaning "Yes, of course," where "natuurlijk" means "naturally."  

• Examples:  
  - "Lust je koffie?" (Do you like coffee?)  
  - "Ja, ik lust wel een appel." (Yes, I like an apple.)  
  - "Natuurlijk ga ik mee." (Of course, I will go along.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Lust je vis?" (Do you like fish?)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch culture, it is common to ask if someone "lust" something before serving food, emphasizing hospitality and consideration for personal preferences.

sentences.nl: Mag het iets meer zijn? — Geen probleem!
sentences.en: Can it be a little more? — No problem!
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• May it something more be? — No problem!

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Mag" is the third person singular of "mogen," meaning "may" or "is allowed to."  
• "Het" is a pronoun meaning "it."  
• "Iets meer" means "something more" or "a bit more."  
• "Zijn" is the infinitive form of "to be." In this context, it acts as the main verb in the question.  
• The word order in the question is typical for Dutch, starting with the verb ("Mag") followed by the subject ("het"), and then the complement.

Examples:  
• Mag ik je helpen? (May I help you?)  
• Mag ik binnenkomen? (May I come in?)  
• Mag het wat sneller? (Can it be a bit faster?)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Mag ik nog wat koffie? (May I have some more coffee?)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch markets or shops, when buying items like cheese or meat, the shopkeeper might ask "Mag het iets meer zijn?" if they have slightly over the weight you requested. It's a polite way of asking if you're okay with the extra amount.

sentences.nl: Dat is dan 9 euro 85.

sentences.nl: Het wisselgeld mag u houden.
sentences.en: You can keep the change.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• The change may you keep.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Het" is a definite article meaning "the."  
• "Wisselgeld" means "change" (as in money returned).  
• "Mag" is the verb "mogen," meaning "may" or "to be allowed to," indicating permission.  
• "U" is the formal "you."  
• "Houden" is the verb "to keep." Here, it is in the infinitive form following "mag."

• Extra Phrases:  
  - "Je mag het boek houden." (You may keep the book.)  
  - "Mag ik hier zitten?" (May I sit here?)  
  - "U kunt het formulier invullen." (You can fill out the form.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Het cadeau mag je openen." (You may open the gift.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, it is common to tip by telling service staff to keep the change rather than adding a percentage to the bill.

sentences.nl: Zo nu hebben we alles.
sentences.en: So now we have everything.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• So now have we everything.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Zo" is an adverb often used to indicate a transition or conclusion, similar to "so" in English.  
• The sentence structure follows the subject-verb-object order: "we" (subject) - "hebben" (verb) - "alles" (object).  
• "Nu" means "now," indicating the current moment.

• Example 1: "Nu zijn we klaar." (Now we are ready.)  
• Example 2: "Zo, dat is geregeld." (So, that is arranged.)

## 3. Create a New Example

sentences.nl: Zullen we nog een toetje kopen? — Maar natuurlijk.
sentences.en: Shall we buy another dessert? — But of course.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Shall we another dessert buy? — But of course.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Zullen" is an auxiliary verb used to form the future tense or make suggestions, similar to "shall" or "will" in English.  
• "Nog een" means "another" or "one more," where "nog" can imply "still" or "more."  
• "Maar natuurlijk" is a common phrase meaning "but of course," used to affirm a suggestion or request.

• Example 1: "Zullen we morgen naar het strand gaan?" (Shall we go to the beach tomorrow?)  
• Example 2: "Wil je nog een kopje koffie?" (Do you want another cup of coffee?)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Zullen we vanavond uit eten gaan?" (Shall we go out to eat tonight?)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch culture, desserts are often an important part of a meal, especially during celebratory occasions or when dining out, making this request a common and light-hearted suggestion.

sentences.nl: Die is hier vlakbij.
sentences.en: That is nearby here.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• That is here nearby.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Die" is a pronoun meaning "that" or "those," often used for things or people already mentioned or understood from context.  
• "Hier" means "here," indicating location.  
• "Vlakbij" is an adverb meaning "nearby" or "close by." It combines "vlak" (flat/level) with "bij" (by/near).  
• Example sentences:  
  - "Dit is vlakbij mijn huis." (This is near my house.)  
  - "De winkel is hier dichtbij." (The store is close by here.)  
  - "Het park is vlakbij." (The park is nearby.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Die winkel is vlakbij het station." (That store is near the station.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, many locations and amenities are conveniently located close to residential areas, as cities and towns are often designed for accessibility on foot or by bicycle.
